name: St. Felix's flood (1530)
headline: A North Sea storm surge on 5 November 1530, 'Evil Saturday', swept away much of Zeeland and Flanders, including the land around Reimerswaal, which was never recovered.
numbers: Low: compilation figure without a traceable contemporary count
timeline: Storm surge on St. Felix's day breaks dikes across Zeeland and Flanders.
Oost-Watering on Zuid-Beveland is lost except the town of Reimerswaal; the 'Drowned Land of Reimerswaal' remains under water.

What happened: On Saturday 5 November 1530, St. Felix's day, a North Sea storm surge broke through dikes in Zeeland and Flanders. Large parts of the region were washed away, including nearly all of Oost-Watering on Zuid-Beveland; the area became the Verdronken Land van Reimerswaal ('drowned land of Reimerswaal'), and the town itself was later abandoned. The day was remembered as kwade zaterdag, 'Evil Saturday'.
Why North Sea surges are so dangerous: The southern North Sea is shallow and narrows toward the Strait of Dover. When a deep low-pressure system drives north-westerly winds down its length at high tide, water piles against the Dutch and Flemish coasts. Much of the land behind the dikes was low-lying reclaimed peatland, so once breached it could not easily be won back.
The death toll and why it is uncertain: The figure of 'more than 100,000' killed appears in modern summaries with the word 'reportedly' and no primary count; the population of the affected area at the time makes so high a toll hard to reconcile. Sixteenth-century chroniclers often reported very large round numbers. We rate it low confidence.
